content: Glomeromycota, informally known as glomeromycetes, is one of the six currently recognized phyla within the kingdom Fungi, comprising approximately 200 described species. With the exception of Geosiphon pyriformis, which forms an endocytobiotic association with Nostoc cyanobacteria, all other species are believed to form arbuscular mycorrhizas with the roots of terrestrial plants. However, this has not been definitively demonstrated for all species. The majority of evidence suggests that members of Glomeromycota are obligate biotrophs, relying on symbiotic relationships with land plants (or Nostoc in the case of Geosiphon) for their carbon and energy needs. Nonetheless, recent circumstantial evidence indicates that some species may have the capacity to exist independently. Arbuscular mycorrhizal species are terrestrial and are widely distributed in soils across the globe, where they form symbiotic relationships with the roots of most plant species. They are also found in wetlands, including salt marshes, and in association with epiphytic plants. Reproduction Glomeromycota fungi generally possess coenocytic mycelia, though they may occasionally exhibit sparse septation. They reproduce asexually through the blastic development of the hyphal tip, which produces spores ranging in diameter from 80 to 500 μm. In some species, complex spores develop within a terminal sac-like structure. Phylogeny Initial studies of Glomeromycota were based on the morphology of soil-borne sporocarps (spore clusters) found in or near colonized plant roots. Features such as spore wall morphology, size, shape, color, hyphal attachment, and reactions to staining compounds were used to construct a phylogeny. Superficial similarities initially led to the placement of the genus Glomus within the unrelated family Endogonaceae. However, broader reviews clarified the confusion surrounding sporocarp morphology, and Glomeromycota was first proposed within the genera Acaulospora and Gigaspora before being assigned its own order, which included the families Glomaceae (now Glomeraceae), Acaulosporaceae, and Gigasporaceae. The advent of molecular techniques has significantly revised this classification, confirming the monophyly of the group. Analysis of small subunit (SSU) rRNA sequences revealed that Glomeromycota shares a common ancestor with the Dikarya, while the Endogonaceae are late-branching members of the chytrid lineage. Spores resembling those of Glomus were found to belong to other deeply divergent lineages and were placed in the orders Paraglomerales and Archaeosporales. This new classification includes the family Geosiphonaceae within the Archaeosporales, which currently contains a single fungus that forms endosymbiotic associations with the cyanobacterium Nostoc punctiforme and produces spores characteristic of this phylum. Research in this area remains incomplete, and some members of Glomus may be better suited to different genera or families. Molecular Biology The biochemical and genetic characterization of Glomeromycota has been hindered by their biotrophic nature, which complicates laboratory cultivation. This challenge was eventually overcome through the use of root cultures. The first mycorrhizal gene to be sequenced was the small subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU rRNA), a highly conserved gene commonly used in phylogenetic studies. This gene was isolated from spores of each taxonomic group and amplified using polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A molecular clock approach, based on the substitution rates of SSU sequences, was employed to estimate the divergence time of these fungi. Molecular analysis determined that Glomeromycota is between 462 and 353 million years old. This data supports the long-standing hypothesis that these fungi played a crucial role in the colonization of land by plants.
